<explanation>
Below is a tailored plan for drawing a comprehensive system‐design diagram of JAX. It shows how the major pieces (Python API, transformation engine, compiler, runtime, backends, CI/CD, etc.) fit together and interact.

1. Identify project type and purpose  
   - JAX is an open-source Python library for high-performance numerical computing.  
   - It provides composable transformations (grad, jit, vmap) on NumPy-style array code and compiles to XLA for execution on CPU, GPU, and TPU.  

2. Top-level components (from file tree & README)  
   • Python-level interface (“jax” package)  
     – jax/api.py, jax/_src/api.py for user-facing functions (grad, jit, vmap)  
     – jax.numpy, jax.scipy, jax.lax, jax.experimental subpackages  
   • Core transformation engine  
     – interpreters (ad.py, batching.py, mlir.py, pxla.py under jax/_src/interpreters)  
     – jaxpr IR representation and passes (jax/core.py, jax/_src/jaxpr_util.py)  
   • XLA integration  
     – translation to XLA HLO (mlir bridge under jax/_src/compilation_cache, compiler.py, custom_partitioning)  
   • Runtime support (jaxlib C++ extensions)  
     – jaxlib/python entry points (py_array.cc, py_client.cc)  
     – device-specific kernels in jaxlib/cpu, jaxlib/gpu, jaxlib/rocm, jaxlib/triton  
   • Hardware backends  
     – CPU via Eigen/LAPACK  
     – NVIDIA GPU via CUDA/cuBLAS/cuDNN  
     – Google TPU via XLA TPU runtime  
     – AMD GPU via ROCm plugin  
     – Apple/Intel GPUs via community plugins  
   • Build & packaging  
     – Bazel and pyproject.toml / setup.py for source builds  
     – build_wheel.py, build/rocm Dockerfiles, jax_plugins for cuda/rocm  
     – CI/CD workflows (.github/workflows, ci/, build/rocm/)  
   • Examples, benchmarks, tutorials, docs, tests  
     – examples/ and benchmarks/ for usage patterns  
     – docs/, cloud_tpu_colabs/ for guidance  
     – tests/ and benchmarks/ for quality & performance  

3. Relationships & data flow  
   1. User writes Python code importing jax (box: “User code”)  
   2. Python API layer (grad, jit, vmap) calls into the transformation engine (arrows)  
   3. Transformation engine converts functions to jaxpr IR, applies autodiff and vectorization passes  
   4. Transformed IR is lowered to XLA HLO via the MLIR bridge  
   5. XLA HLO is compiled just-in-time into device-specific machine code  
   6. jaxlib runtime loads and executes compiled binaries on target hardware (CPU/GPU/TPU)  
   7. Results are returned to Python and wrapped as DeviceArray objects  

4. Architectural patterns & principles  
   - Layered architecture:
     • Python frontend → transformation core → compiler → runtime → hardware  
   - Pluggable backends:
     • Abstract dispatch in jax/_src/dispatch.py → concrete plugin in jaxlib  
   - Separation of concerns:
     • Pure Python transformations and IR manipulation  
     • Low-level kernels and memory management in C++  
   - Build isolation:
     • Bazel for C++ and Python integration  
     • Docker/rocm/CI scripts for multi-platform support  

5. How to tailor this diagram (open-source library focus)  
   - Highlight core extensibility points:
     • interpreter registration, custom primitives (jax.custom_vjp, custom_jvp)  
     • plugin mechanism (jax_plugins for cuda/rocm)  
   - Show integration with external tools:
     • XLA compiler project under third_party/xla  
     • MLIR dialects in jax/_src/export and jax/extend/mlir  
   - Emphasize community & continuous integration:
     • .github/workflows building wheels for multiple platforms  
     • ci/ scripts for Bazel test matrices  

6. Diagram elements to include  
   - Boxes for each major component:
     • User code  
     • Python API  
     • Transformation engine (jaxpr / interpreters)  
     • MLIR / XLA bridge  
     • jaxlib runtime & kernel libraries  
     • Hardware backends (CPU, GPU, TPU)  
     • Build & CI system  
   - Arrows for data/control flow:
     • Python calls → IR generation → compilation → execution  
     • Runtime dispatch → kernel invocation → device memory  
   - Color coding or shapes:
     • Python code (light blue)  
     • IR & compiler layers (green)  
     • C++ runtime & kernels (orange)  
     • Hardware & plugins (gray)  
     • Build/CI (purple)  
   - Clear labels:
     • Functions (grad, jit, vmap)  
     • IR formats (jaxpr, HLO)  
     • Plugins (jaxlib, jax_plugins)  
     • External systems (XLA, Bazel, CI/CD)  

7. Key tips  
   - Be very detailed: break the “jax” box into subcomponents (api vs core vs interpreters).  
   - Capture plugin hooks: dispatch → custom backend.  
   - Show both static relationships (dependencies) and dynamic flows (data through transforms).  
   - Don’t overthink—represent every major directory group as a component box, then draw arrows for “how code travels.”  

Using these guidelines, the principal engineer can craft a layered, color-coded diagram that clearly shows how user code flows through JAX’s Python API into its transformation core, gets lowered via XLA, executes in jaxlib on various backends, and how the build/CI system ties it all together.
